records.question: Which agencies collaborate in the Coral Reef Advisory Group (CRAG)?
records.ground_truth_answer: The Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR); the Department of Commerce (DOC; including AS Coastal Management Program & Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary); the American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency (EPA); the American Samoa Community College (ASCC); and the National Park of American Samoa (NPS).
ground_truth_chunks: The group is a collaboration of five local agencies: the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR), the Department of Commerce (DOC; including AS Coastal Management Program & Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary), the American Samoa Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the American Samoa Community College (ASCC), and the National Park of American Samoa (NPS).

Member agencies work together by mutual consensus to manage coral reefs with the vision "to protect and conserve reefs for the benefit of the people of American Samoa, the United States, and the world".

records.question: What is the reef flat and when can it be snorkeled?
records.ground_truth_answer: The reef flat is a hard, nearly flat reef that begins right at the low tide line; it is the area people walk out on at low tide and it can be snorkeled at mid to high tide.

records.question: What role do zooxanthellae play in the nutrition of coral polyps?
records.ground_truth_answer: Zooxanthellae are tiny, single-celled algae in coral tissues that convert sunlight into food and leak most of that food out, which is taken up by the coral polyp and helps the coral to grow.
ground_truth_chunks: Corals are very unusual among animals, in that their tissues contain tiny, single-celled plants or algae, called "zooxanthellae" (Fig. 3).

When sunlight strikes these tiny algae cells, they convert it into food, just like the leaves of plants on land. The algae cells leak most of that food out, which is taken up by the coral polyp, helping the coral to grow.
